```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
# Solution slides run the real code. The data lives next to the notebooks.
library("ggsci")
library("MASS")
library("scales")
library("tidymodels")
library("tidyverse")
library("patchwork")
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = "../notebooksanddata")
options(width = 50, tibble.print_min = 4, tibble.print_max = 4, pillar.max_extra_cols = 4)

# Theme functions from Lab 2, as in the notebook's setup chunk, with larger text for the screen
theme_histogram <- function() {
  theme_minimal(base_size = 15) +
    theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())
}
theme_boxplot <- function() {
  theme_minimal(base_size = 15) +
    theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(), legend.position = "none")
}
theme_bar <- function() {
  theme_minimal(base_size = 15) +
    theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())
}
theme_scatter <- function() {
  theme_minimal(base_size = 15) +
    theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), legend.position = "bottom")
}
red <- "#E2001A"; dark <- "#8C0014"; pink <- "#F28A94"; grey <- "#6B6B6B"
```

```{r}
#| label: data
#| include: false
students <- read_csv("data/students-data-cleaned.csv")
adv <- read_csv("advertising.csv")

# Concept block: sales ~ TV
ols <- linear_reg() |> fit(sales ~ TV, data = adv)
b0 <- coef(ols$fit)[[1]]; b1 <- coef(ols$fit)[[2]]
adv_aug <- augment(ols, new_data = adv)
rss_ols <- sum(adv_aug$.resid^2)
rss_mean <- sum((adv$sales - mean(adv$sales))^2)
first <- adv_aug[1, ]

# Lab: split, fit, lasso
set.seed(123)
students_split <- initial_split(students, prop = 0.75)
students_train <- training(students_split)
students_test <- testing(students_split)
mv_model <- linear_reg() |> fit(final_grade ~ ., data = students_train)
reg_metrics <- metric_set(rsq, rmse)
lasso_model <-
  linear_reg(penalty = 0.1, mixture = 1) |>
  set_engine("glmnet") |>
  fit(final_grade ~ ., data = students_train)

# ---- Step-by-step visuals for the concept slides. Each helper draws the plot up to step k; the slide
# ---- stacks one version per step, so every click adds one element to the picture.
adv_base <- function(pts = TRUE) {
  p <- ggplot(adv, aes(TV, sales)) +
    coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 300), ylim = c(0, 28)) +
    theme_scatter() +
    labs(x = "TV advertising budget ($1,000s)", y = "Sales (1,000s of units)")
  if (pts) p <- p + geom_point(alpha = 0.55, colour = grey)
  p
}
lines3 <- tibble(line = c("A", "B", "C"), intercept = c(11, b0, 2), slope = c(0.02, b1, 0.08),
                 col = c("#1F4E79", red, "#1D7A46"))
line_step <- function(k) {
  p <- adv_base()
  if (k >= 2) {
    p <- p +
      geom_abline(data = lines3, aes(intercept = intercept, slope = slope, colour = line), linewidth = 1.2) +
      annotate("label", x = 292, y = lines3$intercept + lines3$slope * 292, label = lines3$line,
               colour = lines3$col, fontface = "bold", size = 5) +
      scale_colour_manual(values = c(A = "#1F4E79", B = red, C = "#1D7A46"), guide = "none")
  }
  p
}
resid_step <- function(k) {
  p <- adv_base(pts = FALSE)
  if (k >= 5) p <- p + geom_segment(data = adv_aug, aes(xend = TV, yend = .pred), colour = pink, alpha = 0.7)
  p <- p + geom_point(alpha = 0.55, colour = grey) +
    geom_abline(intercept = b0, slope = b1, colour = red, linewidth = 1.2)
  if (k >= 2) p <- p + geom_point(data = first, colour = dark, size = 4) +
    annotate("label", x = first$TV, y = first$sales + 2.4, label = paste0("budget ", first$TV, ", sold ", first$sales),
             colour = dark, fontface = "bold", size = 3.8)
  if (k >= 3) p <- p + geom_point(data = first, aes(y = .pred), colour = red, size = 4, shape = 21, fill = "white", stroke = 1.5) +
    annotate("label", x = first$TV, y = first$.pred - 2.4, label = paste0("line says ", sprintf("%.1f", first$.pred)),
             colour = red, fontface = "bold", size = 3.8)
  if (k >= 4) p <- p + geom_segment(data = first, aes(xend = TV, yend = .pred), colour = dark, linewidth = 1.6) +
    annotate("label", x = first$TV - 8, y = (first$sales + first$.pred) / 2, label = paste0("residual = +", round(first$.resid, 1)),
             hjust = 1, colour = dark, fontface = "bold", size = 3.8)
  p
}
flat_step <- function(k) {
  p <- adv_base(pts = FALSE)
  if (k >= 2) p <- p + geom_segment(data = adv, aes(xend = TV, yend = mean(sales)), colour = pink, alpha = 0.6)
  p + geom_point(alpha = 0.5, colour = grey, size = 1.2) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = mean(adv$sales), colour = "#1F4E79", linewidth = 1.2) +
    labs(x = "TV budget", y = "Sales")
}
cand <- tibble(slope = c(0.01, 0.07, 0.03, b1)) |>
  mutate(intercept = mean(adv$sales) - slope * mean(adv$TV),
         rss = map2_dbl(intercept, slope, ~ sum((adv$sales - (.x + .y * adv$TV))^2)),
         lab = paste0("slope ", round(slope, 3), "\nRSS ", format(round(rss), big.mark = ",")),
         best = slope == b1)
bowl <- tibble(slope = seq(0, 0.1, by = 0.0005)) |>
  mutate(intercept = mean(adv$sales) - slope * mean(adv$TV),
         rss = map2_dbl(intercept, slope, ~ sum((adv$sales - (.x + .y * adv$TV))^2)))
bowl_step <- function(k) {
  c_k <- cand[seq_len(min(k, 4)), ]
  cols <- scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = red, `FALSE` = "#1F4E79"), guide = "none")
  left <- ggplot(adv, aes(TV, sales)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.35, colour = grey, size = 1.2) +
    geom_abline(data = c_k, aes(intercept = intercept, slope = slope, colour = best), linewidth = 1.1) +
    geom_label(data = c_k, aes(x = 2, y = intercept, label = lab, colour = best),
               hjust = 0, size = 3.2, label.size = 0, fontface = "bold") +
    cols + coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 300), ylim = c(0, 30)) + theme_scatter() + labs(x = "TV budget", y = "Sales")
  right <- ggplot(bowl, aes(slope, rss)) +
    (if (k >= 5) geom_line(colour = "#1F4E79", linewidth = 1.2)) +
    geom_point(data = c_k, aes(colour = best), size = 3.5) +
    (if (k >= 5) geom_vline(xintercept = b1, linetype = "dashed", colour = red)) +
    (if (k >= 5) annotate("label", x = b1, y = max(bowl$rss) * 0.85, label = paste0("smallest RSS\nslope = ", round(b1, 4)),
                          colour = red, fontface = "bold", size = 3.6)) +
    cols + scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma()) +
    coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 0.1), ylim = range(bowl$rss)) + theme_scatter() + labs(x = "Slope of the line", y = "RSS")
  left + right
}
r2_step <- function(k) {
  p <- adv_base(pts = FALSE)
  if (k == 1) {
    p + geom_segment(data = adv, aes(xend = TV, yend = mean(sales)), colour = pink, alpha = 0.6) +
      geom_point(alpha = 0.5, colour = grey, size = 1.2) +
      geom_hline(yintercept = mean(adv$sales), colour = "#1F4E79", linewidth = 1.2) +
      labs(title = paste0("Flat line: TSS = ", format(round(rss_mean), big.mark = ",")))
  } else {
    p + geom_segment(data = adv_aug, aes(xend = TV, yend = .pred), colour = pink, alpha = 0.6) +
      geom_point(alpha = 0.5, colour = grey, size = 1.2) +
      geom_abline(intercept = b0, slope = b1, colour = red, linewidth = 1.2) +
      labs(title = paste0("Line B: RSS = ", format(round(rss_ols), big.mark = ",")))
  }
}
dial <- map_dfr(c(0, 0.1, 1), function(p) {
  linear_reg(penalty = p, mixture = 1) |>
    set_engine("glmnet") |>
    fit(final_grade ~ ., data = students_train) |>
    tidy() |>
    filter(term != "(Intercept)") |>
    mutate(penalty = p)
})
dial_lab <- dial |>
  group_by(penalty) |>
  summarise(n = sum(estimate != 0)) |>
  mutate(label = paste0("penalty = ", penalty, if_else(penalty == 0, " (OLS)", ""), "\n", n, " of 67 coefficients non-zero"))
dial_step <- function(k) {
  dial |>
    left_join(dial_lab, by = "penalty") |>
    mutate(label = factor(label, levels = dial_lab$label), term = fct_reorder(term, abs(estimate))) |>
    filter(penalty <= c(0, 0.1, 1)[k]) |>
    ggplot(aes(abs(estimate), term, fill = estimate == 0)) +
    geom_col() +
    facet_wrap(~ label, drop = FALSE) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = red, `TRUE` = grey), guide = "none") +
    coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 2.2)) +
    theme_bar() +
    theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13)) +
    labs(x = "Size of the coefficient", y = "One bar per coefficient (67)")
}
pen_step <- function(k) {
  d <- tibble(beta = seq(-1.5, 1.5, by = 0.01)) |>
    mutate(Lasso = abs(beta), Ridge = beta^2) |>
    pivot_longer(-beta, names_to = "penalty", values_to = "cost")
  if (k < 2) d <- filter(d, penalty == "Lasso")
  ggplot(d, aes(beta, cost, colour = penalty)) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 1.4) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(Lasso = red, Ridge = "#1F4E79"), limits = c("Lasso", "Ridge"), drop = FALSE) +
    annotate("label", x = 0, y = 1.45, label = "the kink: the push toward 0\nnever lets up", colour = red, size = 3.6, fontface = "bold") +
    (if (k >= 2) annotate("label", x = 0, y = -0.2, label = "flat: the push fades to nothing", colour = "#1F4E79", size = 3.6, fontface = "bold")) +
    coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-0.3, 1.6)) +
    theme_scatter() +
    labs(x = "A coefficient β", y = "Rent charged", colour = NULL)
}
```

## Warm-up 1 of 3

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="on">Concept</span><span>1 · EDA</span><span>2 · Hypothesis</span><span>3 · ML</span><span>4 · Residuals</span><span>5 · Lasso</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```

::: {.ask}
A rule predicts a grade as **10 + 0.5 × hours of study**. A student studies 4 hours a week. What grade does the rule predict?
:::

```{=html}
<div class="mcq">
  <div class="opt"><b>A</b>10.5</div>
  <div class="opt right"><b>B</b>12</div>
  <div class="opt"><b>C</b>14</div>
  <div class="opt"><b>D</b>I'm not sure how to read the rule</div>
  <div class="fragment why"><b>B.</b> 10 + 0.5 × 4 = 10 + 2 = 12. Reading a rule like this is all the arithmetic we need today.</div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
Timing: the concept block is 15 minutes; the three warm-up questions take the first 3. Hands up for each option, then click to reveal. Don't explain beyond the one line on the slide; the concept block does that.

- Gauge: if a good share pick A, C or D, go slowly through "What is a model?" and "The equation, piece by piece", and click through every arithmetic line. If nearly everyone says B, those two slides can be brisk.
:::

## Warm-up 2 of 3

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="on">Concept</span><span>1 · EDA</span><span>2 · Hypothesis</span><span>3 · ML</span><span>4 · Residuals</span><span>5 · Lasso</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```

::: {.ask}
How does linear regression choose *which* line to draw through the points?
:::

```{=html}
<div class="mcq">
  <div class="opt"><b>A</b>The line that passes through the most points</div>
  <div class="opt"><b>B</b>The line whose gaps to the points add up to zero</div>
  <div class="opt right"><b>C</b>The line whose squared gaps to the points are as small as possible</div>
  <div class="opt"><b>D</b>I've never thought about it</div>
  <div class="fragment why"><b>C.</b> Ordinary least squares: the smallest sum of squared residuals. B is a trap: many bad lines have gaps that add up to zero.</div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
- Gauge: this is the core of the concept block. If most pick C and can say why, move faster through "Add them up?" and "the bowl" and spend the time on the equation and the code instead. If B or D dominate, take the full twelve minutes.
:::

## Warm-up 3 of 3

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="on">Concept</span><span>1 · EDA</span><span>2 · Hypothesis</span><span>3 · ML</span><span>4 · Residuals</span><span>5 · Lasso</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```

::: {.ask}
A house-price model has R² = 0.65. What does that mean?
:::

```{=html}
<div class="mcq">
  <div class="opt"><b>A</b>65% of the model's predictions are correct</div>
  <div class="opt right"><b>B</b>The features (such as floor area) explain 65% of the variation in house prices</div>
  <div class="opt"><b>C</b>The model's error is 65% smaller than a perfect model's</div>
  <div class="opt"><b>D</b>I haven't met R² before</div>
  <div class="fragment why"><b>B.</b> R² is about variation, not about how many predictions are "right": a regression prediction is almost never exactly right. The remaining 35% is left in the residuals.</div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
- Gauge: R² and RMSE come up in every lab from now on. If most pick B, the two "How good is the line?" slides are a quick reminder. If A is popular (the classic misreading) or D, slow down there and keep the word "variation" in the room.
- Three answers, three dials: arithmetic (slides 5 and 10), least squares (slides 6 to 9), fit measures (slides 11 and 12).
:::

## What is a model?

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="on">Concept</span><span>1 · EDA</span><span>2 · Hypothesis</span><span>3 · ML</span><span>4 · Residuals</span><span>5 · Lasso</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```

:::: {.columns style="align-items:start"}

::: {.column width="58%"}
A model is a **rule** that turns inputs into a prediction. Made up for now: a grade from study hours and past failures.

```{=html}
<div class="calc sm">
  <div class="hl"><span class="cl">The rule</span><span class="cx">grade = 10 + 0.5 × hours − 2 × failures</span></div>
  <div class="fragment"><span class="cl">One student</span><span class="cx">6 hours a week, 1 past failure</span></div>
  <div class="fragment"><span class="cl">Plug in</span><span class="cx">10 + 0.5 × 6 − 2 × 1 = 10 + 3 − 2</span></div>
  <div class="fragment hl"><span class="cl">Prediction</span><span class="cx">= 11</span></div>
  <div class="fragment"><span class="cl">Actual grade</span><span class="cx">13</span></div>
  <div class="fragment hl"><span class="cl">Residual</span><span class="cx">13 − 11 = +2 <small>the rule guessed 2 points too low</small></span></div>
</div>
```
:::

::: {.column width="42%"}
::: {.fragment}
::: {.card .dark}
[Where do 10, 0.5 and −2 come from?]{.ct}
The numbers in the rule are its **coefficients**. Someone has to choose them.

An **algorithm** is a recipe for choosing them from data. Today's: **ordinary least squares**, built from scratch in the next five slides.
:::
:::
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
Timing: concept block, 12 minutes across this slide and the next ten. Click through the arithmetic one line at a time and ask the questions before showing the answers.

- A model is nothing more than a rule. Numbers in, prediction out. I made this rule up; nobody has fitted anything yet.
- One student, plug in, prediction 11, actual 13, residual +2. Make sure everyone can follow the arithmetic: nothing harder than this happens all day.
- The numbers in the rule are the coefficients. Someone had to pick them. The recipe for picking them from data is the algorithm, and that is what we build now.
- The notebook has the same idea written as an R function with three inputs; it isn't needed to follow the slides.
:::

- Line B on its own. Click: one market lights up, budget 230.1, sold 22.1. Click: where the line would put it, 18.0. Click: the gap between the two is the residual, +4.1.
- Click: the definition and the sign. Click: all 200 residuals. 200 numbers. We need one. Ask the room how they'd combine them before moving on.
:::

## Add them up?

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="on">Concept</span><span>1 · EDA</span><span>2 · Hypothesis</span><span>3 · ML</span><span>4 · Residuals</span><span>5 · Lasso</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```

::: {.cards .c2}
::: {.card .line}
[Just add the residuals]{.ct}

::: {.r-stack}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 2.3
flat_step(1)
```

::: {.fragment fragment-index=0}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 2.3
flat_step(2)
```
:::
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=0}
A flat line at the average is clearly bad, yet its residuals add up to **exactly 0**: positives and negatives cancel.
:::
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
::: {.card}
[Square first, then add]{.ct}

```{=html}
<div class="calc sm">
  <div><span class="cl">Market 1</span><span class="cx">`r sprintf("%+.1f", adv_aug$.resid[1])`&thinsp;² = `r round(adv_aug$.resid[1]^2, 1)`</span></div>
  <div class="fragment" data-fragment-index="2"><span class="cl">Market 2</span><span class="cx">`r sprintf("%+.1f", adv_aug$.resid[2])`&thinsp;² = `r round(adv_aug$.resid[2]^2, 1)`</span></div>
  <div class="fragment" data-fragment-index="3"><span class="cl">Market 5</span><span class="cx">`r sprintf("%+.1f", adv_aug$.resid[5])`&thinsp;² = `r round(adv_aug$.resid[5]^2, 1)` <small>negative, but its square is positive</small></span></div>
  <div class="fragment hl" data-fragment-index="4"><span class="cl">All 200</span><span class="cx">RSS = `r format(round(rss_ols), big.mark = ",")` <small>residual sum of squares</small></span></div>
</div>
```

::: {.fragment fragment-index=5}
Flat line: `r format(round(rss_mean), big.mark = ",")`. Line B: `r format(round(rss_ols), big.mark = ",")`. **Lower is better**, and one miss of 4 now costs more than two misses of 2.
:::
:::
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
- Ask the room first. Someone says "add them". Click: the flat line's residuals appear; a terrible line scores zero, because the misses above and below cancel.
- Fix: square each residual first. Click through three markets, then the total: the residual sum of squares, RSS. That's our score for a line. Lower is better.
- Squaring also makes one big miss cost more than several small ones (16 against 8), which is usually what we want.
:::

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="on">Concept</span><span>1 · EDA</span><span>2 · Hypothesis</span><span>3 · ML</span><span>4 · Residuals</span><span>5 · Lasso</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```


::: {.cards .c2 style="margin-top:0.2em"}
::: {.fragment fragment-index=3}
::: {.card .compact .dark}
[Ordinary least squares (OLS)]{.ct}
The line with the **smallest sum of squared residuals**. That's the whole algorithm.
:::
:::
::: {.fragment fragment-index=4}
::: {.card .compact}
[You don't have to try every line]{.ct}
For linear models a formula jumps straight to the bottom of the bowl. Later models really do walk downhill.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Each click tries one more line on the left and adds its RSS as a dot on the right.

- Too flat: RSS high. Too steep: high again. Closer: lower. The best one: lowest. Click: the full curve. A bowl. The bottom of the bowl is the best line.
- That's the algorithm: least squares means the smallest sum of squared residuals.
- For linear models there's a closed formula for the bottom, so nothing is actually tried. For other models later in the course the computer does walk downhill, step by step.
:::

## The equation, piece by piece

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="on">Concept</span><span>1 · EDA</span><span>2 · Hypothesis</span><span>3 · ML</span><span>4 · Residuals</span><span>5 · Lasso</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```

::: {.anatomy .eq}
```{=html}
<p class="anat-code"><span class="tok">ŷ</span> = <span class="tok">β₀</span> + <span class="tok">β₁</span> · <span class="tok">x</span></p>
```

1. **The prediction.** The hat means "our estimate", as opposed to the real *y*. Spoken "y-hat".
2. **The intercept.** The prediction when *x* is 0.
3. **The slope.** The change in the prediction when *x* goes up by **one unit**.
4. **The feature.** The input we know. Also called predictor or independent variable.
:::

```{=html}
<div class="calc sm">
  <div><span class="cl">Fitted line</span><span class="cx">sales = `r round(b0, 2)` + `r round(b1, 4)` × TV <small>every extra $1,000 on TV adds about `r round(b1 * 1000)` units</small></span></div>
  <div class="fragment"><span class="cl">Market 1</span><span class="cx">TV = `r first$TV`</span></div>
  <div class="fragment"><span class="cl">Plug in</span><span class="cx">`r round(b0, 2)` + `r round(b1, 4)` × `r first$TV` = `r round(b0, 2)` + `r round(b1 * first$TV, 2)`</span></div>
  <div class="fragment hl"><span class="cl">Prediction</span><span class="cx">ŷ = `r sprintf("%.1f", first$.pred)` <small>the "line says" number from three slides ago</small></span></div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
- Same thing in symbols. Greek letters are just names for the numbers the algorithm chooses; "beta" is the convention for coefficients.
- Read the slope out loud: "for every one-unit increase in x, the prediction changes by beta-one". That sentence is the interpretation of every coefficient you'll ever see.
- Hover a part to highlight its explanation.
:::

## More than one feature

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="on">Concept</span><span>1 · EDA</span><span>2 · Hypothesis</span><span>3 · ML</span><span>4 · Residuals</span><span>5 · Lasso</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```

::: {.anatomy .eq}
```{=html}
<p class="anat-code">ŷ = β₀ + <span class="tok">β₁ x₁</span> + <span class="tok">β₂ x₂</span> + … + <span class="tok">βₚ xₚ</span></p>
```

1. **One coefficient per feature.** Each β: the change in the prediction when *that* feature rises by 1, **with the others held fixed**.
2. **Still a line**, just in more dimensions. Same squared residuals, same bowl, same bottom.
3. ***p* features, *p* slopes.** Today: 30 columns, 67 coefficients.
:::

::: {.card .compact style="margin-top:0.5em"}
[Why 67 coefficients from 30 features?]{.ct}
Text columns become 0/1 columns: `higher` yes/no becomes `higheryes` (1 for yes). A feature with 4 categories gets 3 such columns, one for each category except the first, the **reference**.
:::

::: {.notes}
- Adding features adds terms. Nothing else changes.
- Text columns are turned into 0/1 columns automatically. "higheryes = 3.5" means students who want higher education score 3.5 points higher, other things equal.
- The reference category is the one the others are compared with. It's the first level alphabetically unless you say otherwise.
:::

## How good is the line? R²

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="on">Concept</span><span>1 · EDA</span><span>2 · Hypothesis</span><span>3 · ML</span><span>4 · Residuals</span><span>5 · Lasso</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```

::: {.anatomy .eq}
```{=html}
<p class="anat-code"><span class="tok">R²</span> = 1 − <span class="tok">RSS</span> / <span class="tok">TSS</span></p>
```

1. **Share of the variation explained**: 0 is no better than the mean, 1 is a perfect fit.
2. Squared residuals of **our** line.
3. Squared residuals of the **flat line** at the mean.
:::

:::: {.columns style="align-items:start"}

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.r-stack}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 2.1
r2_step(1)
```

::: {.fragment fragment-index=0}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 2.1
r2_step(2)
```
:::
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{=html}
<div class="calc sm">
  <div><span class="cl">Flat line</span><span class="cx">TSS = `r format(round(rss_mean), big.mark = ",")`</span></div>
  <div class="fragment" data-fragment-index="0"><span class="cl">Line B</span><span class="cx">RSS = `r format(round(rss_ols), big.mark = ",")`</span></div>
  <div class="fragment" data-fragment-index="1"><span class="cl">Divide</span><span class="cx">1 − `r format(round(rss_ols), big.mark = ",")` / `r format(round(rss_mean), big.mark = ",")` = 1 − `r round(rss_ols / rss_mean, 2)`</span></div>
  <div class="fragment hl" data-fragment-index="2"><span class="cl">R²</span><span class="cx">= `r round(glance(ols)$r.squared, 2)` <small>TV explains `r round(100 * glance(ols)$r.squared)`% of the variation</small></span></div>
</div>
```
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
- The first of two numbers you will report for every model from now on.
- Start from the dumbest model: predict the average for everyone. Its squared residuals are the TSS, the total variation to explain. Click: line B's squared residuals, the RSS. Click: the share that's left; one minus that is R².
:::

## How good is the line? RMSE

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="on">Concept</span><span>1 · EDA</span><span>2 · Hypothesis</span><span>3 · ML</span><span>4 · Residuals</span><span>5 · Lasso</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```

::: {.anatomy .eq}
```{=html}
<p class="anat-code"><span class="tok">RMSE</span> = √ <span class="tok">mean( residual² )</span></p>
```

1. **Root mean squared error**: the typical miss, in the **units of the outcome**. An RMSE of 3 on a 0–20 grade means a typical prediction is about 3 points off.
2. Average the squared residuals, then take the square root to undo the squaring.
:::

```{=html}
<div class="calc sm">
  <div class="fragment" data-fragment-index="0"><span class="cl">Advertising</span><span class="cx">RSS = `r format(round(rss_ols), big.mark = ",")` over 200 markets</span></div>
  <div class="fragment" data-fragment-index="1"><span class="cl">Mean</span><span class="cx">`r format(round(rss_ols), big.mark = ",")` / 200 = `r round(rss_ols / 200, 1)` <small>the average squared residual</small></span></div>
  <div class="fragment" data-fragment-index="2"><span class="cl">Root</span><span class="cx">√`r round(rss_ols / 200, 1)` = `r round(sqrt(rss_ols / 200), 1)`</span></div>
  <div class="fragment hl" data-fragment-index="3"><span class="cl">RMSE</span><span class="cx">= `r round(sqrt(rss_ols / 200), 1)` thousand units <small>a typical prediction is about `r round(sqrt(rss_ols / 200) * 1000, -2)` units off</small></span></div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
- R² compares you with guessing the average. RMSE undoes the squaring so the number is in the units of the outcome again, which makes it easier to explain to someone else.
- Click through: total, average, square root. On the students data this will be in grade points.
:::

## The same thing in code

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="on">Concept</span><span>1 · EDA</span><span>2 · Hypothesis</span><span>3 · ML</span><span>4 · Residuals</span><span>5 · Lasso</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```

::: {.anatomy}
```{=html}
<p class="anat-code"><span class="tok">linear_reg()</span> |&gt; <span class="tok">fit(</span><span class="tok">final_grade</span> <span class="tok">~</span> <span class="tok">higher</span>, <span class="tok">data = students</span>)</p>
```

1. **Which kind of model.** A linear one. On its own this fits nothing: it's an empty recipe.
2. **Run the algorithm.** Find the coefficients with the smallest RSS.
3. **The outcome**, *y*: what we want to predict. Left of the tilde.
4. **The tilde** reads as "explained by" or "as a function of". It turns the two sides into a **formula**.
5. **The feature(s)**, *x*: right of the tilde. Several: `higher + failures`. Everything else in the table: `.`
6. **Which table** the columns live in.
:::

::: {.anat-read}
In words: "fit a linear model of `final_grade` explained by `higher`, using the `students` table."
:::

::: {.notes}
- Two steps: say what kind of model you want, then fit it. linear_reg() on its own does nothing.
- The formula is how R writes an equation: outcome, tilde, features. Students will type = instead of ~; the error message mentions "formula".
- The dot is a shortcut for "everything else". We'll see later why that can backfire.
:::

::: {.kicker}
Part 2
:::

Is there an effect? How sure are we? · `summary()` · `~ .`

## Reading `summary()`

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="done">Concept</span><span class="done">1 · EDA</span><span class="on">2 · Hypothesis</span><span>3 · ML</span><span>4 · Residuals</span><span>5 · Lasso</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```

```{=html}
<p class="nbref"><b>Notebook</b> lines 146–152 <span>the hypothesis-testing approach</span><i>run together</i></p>
```

:::: {.columns style="align-items:start"}

::: {.column width="50%"}
```r
linear_reg() |>
  fit(final_grade ~ higher, data = students) |>
  extract_fit_engine() |>
  summary()
```

```{=html}
<table class="mini" style="font-size:0.62em">
<tr><th></th><th>Estimate</th><th>Std. Error</th><th>t value</th><th>Pr(&gt;|t|)</th></tr>
<tr><td>(Intercept)</td><td>8.80</td><td>0.367</td><td>24.0</td><td>&lt;2e-16</td></tr>
<tr><td>higheryes</td><td class="hl">3.48</td><td class="hl">0.388</td><td class="hl">8.96</td><td class="hl">&lt;2e-16</td></tr>
</table>
```

::: {.source-note}
Also printed: Multiple R-squared 0.110. `extract_fit_engine()` pulls the `lm` object out of the tidymodels wrapper so `summary()` can print it.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.fragment}
::: {.card .compact}
[Estimate]{.ct}
The coefficient: students who want higher education score **3.48 points higher**. The intercept, 8.80, is the mean grade of the "no" students.
:::
:::
::: {.fragment}
::: {.card .compact}
[Std. Error]{.ct}
How uncertain the estimate is. Another sample would give a slightly different 3.48.
:::
:::
::: {.fragment}
::: {.card .compact}
[t value and p-value]{.ct}
t = estimate ÷ standard error: 9 standard errors from zero. The p-value: *if the true effect were 0, how surprising would this be?* Extremely.
:::
:::
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
Timing: Part 2, 10 minutes across this slide and the next. Live-code it: run the simple model, then add the dot.

- This is the social scientist's question: is there an effect, and is it bigger than chance would produce? Click through: estimate, uncertainty, p-value.
- The last two lines of the code only pull the lm object out of the tidymodels wrapper so summary() can print it.
- Note the R² of 0.11: a highly significant feature that explains little of the variation. Significant is not the same as predictive. Keep that distinction in the room all day.
:::

## Controlling for everything: `~ .`

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="done">Concept</span><span class="done">1 · EDA</span><span class="on">2 · Hypothesis</span><span>3 · ML</span><span>4 · Residuals</span><span>5 · Lasso</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```

```{=html}
<p class="nbref"><b>Notebook</b> lines 160–165 <span>the multivariable model</span><i>run together</i></p>
```

:::: {.columns style="align-items:start"}

::: {.column width="48%"}
```r
linear_reg() |>
  fit(final_grade ~ ., data = students) |>
  extract_fit_engine() |>
  summary()
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
local({
  op <- options(tibble.print_min = 7, tibble.print_max = 7)
  on.exit(options(op))
  linear_reg() |>
    fit(final_grade ~ ., data = students) |>
    tidy() |>
    filter(p.value < 0.01, term != "(Intercept)") |>
    mutate(across(c(estimate, p.value), ~ signif(.x, 2))) |>
    select(term, estimate, p.value) |>
    print()
})
```

::: {.source-note}
The 7 features with p < 0.01, out of 67 coefficients.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="52%"}
::: {.fragment}
::: {.card .compact}
[`higheryes` halves]{.ct}
From 3.48 to **1.62**, still significant. Part of the raw difference was study time and past failures travelling with the wish for higher education.
:::
:::
::: {.fragment}
::: {.card .compact}
[R² rises to 0.41]{.ct}
Sixty-seven coefficients explain 41% of the variation. Each past failure costs about 1.5 points.
:::
:::
::: {.fragment}
::: {.card .compact .dark}
[Caveat]{.ct}
p-values say which features matter for *explaining* these 649 students. They are **no guarantee** the model predicts well for new students.
:::
:::
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
- Add everything and the "higher" effect halves. Still there, still significant.
- Keep R² = 0.41 in mind. We'll see it again from a different angle in Part 3, and it won't look as good.
- p-hacking: a model that produces significant findings can be chosen while the ones that don't go unreported. The notebook links the Data Falsificada series.
:::

# The machine learning approach {.divider background-color="#8C0014"}

::: {.kicker}
Part 3
:::

Split · fit · evaluate · `initial_split()` · `augment()` · `metric_set()`

## Two questions, two approaches

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="done">Concept</span><span class="done">1 · EDA</span><span class="done">2 · Hypothesis</span><span class="on">3 · ML</span><span>4 · Residuals</span><span>5 · Lasso</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```

::: {.cards .c2}
::: {.card .line}
[Hypothesis testing]{.ct}
**Does `higher` matter? How sure are we?**

Coefficients, standard errors, p-values. Uses **all** the data. Part 2.
:::

::: {.card .dark}
[Machine learning]{.ct}
**How well can we predict a grade we haven't seen?**

Predictions and their error on **new** data. **Splits** the data. Parts 3–5.
:::
:::

::: {.punch}
Same model. Different question. Different workflow.
:::

::: {.notes}
Timing: Part 3 is 18 minutes, coded together: the made-up model 3, why split 2, the split 4, fit and predict 3, evaluate 3, debrief 3.

- Same linear_reg(), same formula. The difference is what we look at and which rows we're allowed to use.
- Hypothesis testing tries to falsify a claim about a cause; machine learning cares about the fit in the aggregate, not any one coefficient.
:::

## A made-up model, in the notebook

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="done">Concept</span><span class="done">1 · EDA</span><span class="done">2 · Hypothesis</span><span class="on">3 · ML</span><span>4 · Residuals</span><span>5 · Lasso</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```


```r
  y <- 1.1 * x1 + 2.2 * x2 + 3.3 * x3
  y
}
```

Three inputs, three coefficients, one output. Nobody fitted it: the numbers are made up, like the grade rule earlier.

## Why split?

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="done">Concept</span><span class="done">1 · EDA</span><span class="done">2 · Hypothesis</span><span class="on">3 · ML</span><span>4 · Residuals</span><span>5 · Lasso</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```

::: {.ask}
You revise with last year's exam paper, then sit… last year's paper again. Is your mark a fair measure of what you learned?
:::

::: {.fragment}
```{=html}
<div class="flow">
  <div class="step ai"><b>649 students</b><small>all the rows</small></div>
  <div class="arrow">→</div>
  <div class="stack">
    <div class="step you"><b>Training set · 486 rows (75%)</b><small>the model is fitted here</small></div>
    <div class="step test"><b>Test set · 163 rows (25%)</b><small>locked away; opened only to score the finished model</small></div>
  </div>
</div>
```

::: {.card .compact .dark style="margin-top:0.5em"}
[Overfitting]{.ct}
Scored on its own training rows, a model flatters itself: it has partly memorised their quirks. The test set is a fresh exam. A big **gap** between the two scores is the warning sign.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
- Let them answer the exam question first. Then click.
- The test set is a fresh exam. We lock it away, fit on the rest, and only open it to score the finished model.
- Today's data are cross-sectional, so a random split is fine. Time series need a different split; later in the course.
:::


1. **Make the random draw repeatable**, so your numbers match the slides.
2. **Decide which rows go where.** A *split object*: a note of which rows are which, **not yet two tables**.
3. **The share for training.** 75% here; 70–80% is typical.
4. **Pull out the training table**: 486 rows.
5. **Pull out the test table**: 163 rows. Don't touch it until the model is finished.
:::

::: {.notes}
- Three steps, four functions, all from the rsample package inside tidymodels.
- Students forget that initial_split() doesn't give you tables yet; printing it shows <Training/Testing/Total>.
- The seed only needs to be set once, but it must run in the same chunk as the split or the numbers will differ.

- Residuals are what the model couldn't explain. If they still have a shape, there's structure left: a curve, a missing variable, or, here, a diagonal streak at the bottom left.
- Ask what the streak is before the exercise; let them find out. (Students who scored 0: the residual is minus the prediction, so they line up on a diagonal. No linear rule reaches them.)
- mvrnorm() builds the simulated data with a chosen correlation. They don't need to understand it.

# Lasso: a penalty for every coefficient {.divider background-color="#8C0014"}

::: {.kicker}
Part 5
:::

Regularisation · λ · hyperparameters · `penalty` · `mixture = 1` · `set_engine("glmnet")`

## The problem with "everything"

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="done">Concept</span><span class="done">1 · EDA</span><span class="done">2 · Hypothesis</span><span class="done">3 · ML</span><span class="done">4 · Residuals</span><span class="on">5 · Lasso</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```

::: {.card .compact}
[67 coefficients, 486 training rows]{.ct}
The model is *free* to use every coefficient, so it does, including the ones that only describe noise in the training rows. R² 0.45 in training, 0.21 on new students.
:::

::: {.ask style="margin-top:0.6em"}
How would you stop a model from using coefficients it doesn't need?
:::

::: {.cards .c2}
::: {.fragment}
::: {.card .compact .line}
[Option 1: by hand]{.ct}
Drop the features with large p-values and refit. Slow, subjective, and the p-values came from the model you're about to change.
:::
:::
::: {.fragment}
::: {.card .compact .dark}
[Option 2: inside the algorithm]{.ct}
Change the score the algorithm minimises so that **every coefficient has a cost**. That's the **lasso**.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Timing: Part 5 is 20 minutes: concept 6 (this slide and the next four), syntax 2, exercise 9, solutions and debrief 3.

- Collect ideas first. "Remove the insignificant ones" is a fine answer and the manual version. The lasso does it automatically, inside the algorithm.
:::

## Charge rent for every coefficient

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="done">Concept</span><span class="done">1 · EDA</span><span class="done">2 · Hypothesis</span><span class="done">3 · ML</span><span class="done">4 · Residuals</span><span class="on">5 · Lasso</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```

::: {.anatomy .eq}
```{=html}
<p class="anat-code">Lasso minimises &nbsp; <span class="tok">RSS</span> + <span class="tok">λ</span> · <span class="tok">Σ |βⱼ|</span></p>
```

1. **Fit the data**, as before. OLS minimised this and nothing else.
2. **Lambda: the price per unit of coefficient.** You choose it. The notebook calls it `penalty`.
3. **The total size of all coefficients**, signs ignored. The bill.
:::

```{=html}
<div class="calc sm">
  <div class="fragment" data-fragment-index="0"><span class="cl">Say λ = 0.1</span><span class="cx">and three coefficients: 1.8, −1.4, 0.05</span></div>
  <div class="fragment" data-fragment-index="1"><span class="cl">Total size</span><span class="cx">|1.8| + |−1.4| + |0.05| = 3.25</span></div>
  <div class="fragment hl" data-fragment-index="2"><span class="cl">The bill</span><span class="cx">0.1 × 3.25 = 0.325 <small>added to the RSS</small></span></div>
  <div class="fragment" data-fragment-index="3"><span class="cl">Drop the 0.05</span><span class="cx">bill falls by 0.005 <small>if the RSS rises by less than that, the model is better off without it</small></span></div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
- Same bowl, plus a bill. The algorithm still minimises one number, but the number now has two parts: how badly you fit, and how much coefficient you're using. Lambda sets the exchange rate between the two.
- Click through the bill for three coefficients. Every coefficient has to earn its place: it is only kept at a size where the improvement in fit is worth the rent. One that barely helps shrinks; one that helps a lot stays large.
:::

## Turning the dial {.nostretch}

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="done">Concept</span><span class="done">1 · EDA</span><span class="done">2 · Hypothesis</span><span class="done">3 · ML</span><span class="done">4 · Residuals</span><span class="on">5 · Lasso</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```

::: {.r-stack}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 3.4
dial_step(1)
```

::: {.fragment fragment-index=0}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 3.4
dial_step(2)
```
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 3.4
dial_step(3)
```
:::
:::

::: {.cards .c3 style="margin-top:0.1em"}
::: {.card .compact}
[λ = 0]{.ct}
No rent. Back to OLS: all 67 coefficients in use, and the overfitting from Part 3.
:::
::: {.fragment fragment-index=0}
::: {.card .compact .dark}
[λ = 0.1]{.ct}
Coefficients shrink, and 27 of them hit **exactly zero**. Feature selection built into the fitting.
:::
:::
::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
::: {.card .compact}
[λ = 1]{.ct}
Only 2 survive. Dial it up further and everything goes to zero: the model predicts the mean for everyone.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Each click turns the dial up one notch: one more panel, one more card.

- Dial up lambda and coefficients drop out one by one. Too little and you're back to overfitting; too much and the model knows nothing. Somewhere in between is a sweet spot, and the bonus exercise looks for it.
- The exact zeros are the point: this is feature selection without anyone choosing.
:::

## Why *exactly* zero?

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="done">Concept</span><span class="done">1 · EDA</span><span class="done">2 · Hypothesis</span><span class="done">3 · ML</span><span class="done">4 · Residuals</span><span class="on">5 · Lasso</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="48%"}
::: {.r-stack}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5.2
#| fig-height: 3.8
pen_step(1)
```

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5.2
#| fig-height: 3.8
pen_step(2)
```
:::
:::
:::

::: {.column width="52%"}
::: {.card .compact}
[Two forces on each coefficient]{.ct}
The **data** pull it away from zero, with a force that weakens as the fit improves. The **penalty** pushes it back toward zero.
:::
::: {.fragment fragment-index=0}
::: {.card .compact .dark}
[The lasso's push is constant]{.ct}
|β| has the same slope everywhere, so the push is **λ, whatever the coefficient's size**. If the data's pull is weaker than λ, the coefficient is pinned at **exactly 0**.
:::
:::
::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
::: {.card .compact .line}
[Ridge, for contrast]{.ct}
β² goes flat near zero, so its push fades as the coefficient shrinks: coefficients get tiny but **never reach zero**. `mixture = 1` picks the lasso, `0` the ridge.
:::
:::
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
- The absolute value is the secret. Its slope is the same size everywhere, so the push toward zero never lets up.
- Click: the ridge penalty for contrast. A squared penalty goes gentle near zero and never finishes the job.
- You don't need the calculus; you need the picture of the kink.
:::

## Parameters and hyperparameters

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="done">Concept</span><span class="done">1 · EDA</span><span class="done">2 · Hypothesis</span><span class="done">3 · ML</span><span class="done">4 · Residuals</span><span class="on">5 · Lasso</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```

::: {.cards .c2}
::: {.card}
[Parameters]{.ct}
The **βs**, 67 of them. Chosen **by the algorithm**, from the data, by minimising the score. Inside the machine.
:::

::: {.card .dark}
[Hyperparameters]{.ct}
**λ** (`penalty`) and `mixture`. Chosen **by you**, before fitting. A knob on the outside of the machine.
:::
:::

::: {.card .line .compact style="margin-top:0.6em"}
[Why can't the data choose λ?]{.ct}
Any λ > 0 makes the *training* fit worse, so the algorithm would always pick 0. Instead: try several values, score each on data the model hasn't seen, keep the best. Today's bonus does it by hand; Lab 5 automates it.
:::

::: {.notes}
- Lambda is a knob on the outside of the machine. The bonus turns the knob by hand; in Lab 5 we automate it with cross-validation.
:::

1. **λ.** The rent per unit of coefficient. 0.1 to start.
2. **Which penalty.** 1 is the lasso, 0 is the ridge, in between mixes them.
3. **Which package computes.** The default, `lm`, can't penalise; `glmnet` can.
4. **Step 2, yours:** `tidy()` gives one row per coefficient. Filter out the zeros.

## Solutions: Part 5 {.solution}

:::: {.walk}

::: {.walk-code}
```r
lasso_model <-
  linear_reg(penalty = 0.1, mixture = 1) |>
  set_engine("glmnet") |>
  fit(final_grade ~ ., data = students_train)

tidy(lasso_model) |>
  filter(estimate != 0)

lasso_model |>
  augment(new_data = students_test) |>
  reg_metrics(truth = final_grade, estimate = .pred)
```

::: {.walk-say}
Fit a lasso with penalty 0.1 on the training rows, look at which coefficients survived, then score it on the test rows.
:::
:::

::: {.walk-out}

::: {.fragment fragment-index=0 lines="1-4"}
::: {.say}
Same `fit()` as before, with a price on coefficients and `glmnet` doing the work. Counting the coefficients: 27 were set to exactly zero, 41 (including the intercept) survived.
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
tidy(lasso_model) |>
  count(zero = estimate == 0)
```
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1 lines="6-7"}
::: {.say}
`tidy()` lists every coefficient; `filter()` keeps the non-zero ones. Sorted by size here: wanting higher education, past failures and school support matter most.
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
local({
  op <- options(tibble.print_min = 6, tibble.print_max = 6)
  on.exit(options(op))
  tidy(lasso_model) |>
    filter(estimate != 0, term != "(Intercept)") |>
    arrange(desc(abs(estimate))) |>
    print()
})
```
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=2 lines="9-11"}
::: {.say}
Exactly the evaluation code from Part 3. On the test set: R² 0.24 and RMSE 2.95, against 0.21 and 3.04 for the model with all 67 coefficients.
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
lasso_model |>
  augment(new_data = students_test) |>
  reg_metrics(truth = final_grade, estimate = .pred)
```
:::

## Bonus: turning the dial by hand

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="done">Concept</span><span class="done">1 · EDA</span><span class="done">2 · Hypothesis</span><span class="done">3 · ML</span><span class="done">4 · Residuals</span><span class="on">5 · Lasso</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="58%"}
```{r}
#| label: sweep
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3.4
lasso <- partial(linear_reg, engine = "glmnet", mixture = 1)
preds <-
  crossing(
    penalty = c(0.0001, 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 0.3, 1),
    nest(students_train, .key = "train"),
    nest(students_test, .key = "test")
  ) |>
  mutate(
    model = map(penalty, ~ lasso(penalty = .x)),
    fit = map2(model, train, ~ fit(.x, final_grade ~ ., data = .y)),
    augmented = map2(fit, test, ~ augment(.x, new_data = .y)),
    rmses = map(augmented, ~ rmse(.x, truth = final_grade, estimate = .pred))
  )
preds |>
  unnest(rmses) |>
  mutate(in_notebook = penalty <= 0.1) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = as.factor(penalty), y = .estimate, group = 1)) +
  geom_line(linetype = "dashed", colour = grey) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = in_notebook), size = 3.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = red, `FALSE` = "#1F4E79"), labels = c(`TRUE` = "notebook grid", `FALSE` = "two more"), name = NULL) +
  theme_scatter() +
  labs(x = "Penalty (λ)", y = "Test-set RMSE")
```
:::

::: {.column width="42%"}
::: {.card .compact}
[The notebook's grid]{.ct}
0.0001, 0.001 and 0.01 are all about 3.03, hardly different from plain OLS. **0.1 is best** at 2.95.
:::
::: {.card .compact .line}
[Two more, past the grid]{.ct}
0.3 is worse again (3.04, with only 14 coefficients) and 1 is bad (3.29, with 2). A bowl again, this time scored on test data.
:::
::: {.card .compact .dark}
[That's tuning]{.ct}
Turn the knob, score on data the model hasn't seen, keep the best setting. Lab 5 automates it.
:::
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
- The bonus chunk fits one lasso per penalty with nested tibbles and map2(); students only need to run it and read the plot.
- The curve has a bottom, like the RSS bowl, but this time the score is on test data. That's what tuning a hyperparameter means.
:::

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="done">Concept</span><span class="done">1 · EDA</span><span class="done">2 · Hypothesis</span><span class="done">3 · ML</span><span class="done">4 · Residuals</span><span class="done">5 · Lasso</span><span class="on">Wrap-up</span></div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="checks" style="grid-template-columns:1fr">
  <div><b>1</b><span>Ordinary least squares picks the line with the <strong>smallest sum of squared residuals</strong>. A coefficient is the change in the prediction when its feature rises by one unit, other things equal</span></div>
  <div><b>2</b><span><strong>Split first.</strong> Fit on the training set, score on the test set. The gap between the two scores is overfitting</span></div>
  <div><b>3</b><span><code>linear_reg() |&gt; fit()</code> · <code>augment()</code> · <code>metric_set(rsq, rmse)</code> is the workflow for every model from now on</span></div>
  <div><b>4</b><span>The lasso adds a <strong>price per coefficient</strong>. λ is a hyperparameter you set; coefficients that aren't worth the rent go to exactly zero</span></div>
</div>
```

**Question:** which of the 30 features would you have bet on before today? Did the lasso agree?
